workhead.title: Reliques of Ancient English Poetry. Volume the Second

source.title: Reliques of Ancient English Poetry; consisting of Old Heroic Ballads, Songs, and other Pieces of our earlier Poets, together with some few of later Date

notes.note: Percy oplyser, at teksten er sammensat med rettelser efter to afskrifter eller tryk, hvoraf det ene står i The golden garland of princely delights. Han angiver ingen forfatter.

body.poetry:
My Phillida, adieu love! For evermore farewel! Ay me! I've lost my true love, And thus I ring her knell, Ding dong, ding dong, ding dong, My Phillida is dead! I'll stick a branch of willow At my fair Phillis' head.
For my fair Phillida Our bridal bed was made: But 'stead of silkes so gay, She in her shroud is laid. Ding, &c.
Her corpse shall be attended By maides in fair array, Till the obsequies are ended, And she is wrapt in clay. Ding, &c.
Her herse it shall be carried By youths, that do excell; And when that she is buried, I thus will ring her knell, Ding, &c.
A garland shall be framed By art and natures skill, Of sundry-colour'd flowers, In token of good-willIt is a custom in many parts of England, to carry a flowery garland before the corpse of a woman who dies unmarried.: Ding, &c.
And sundry-colour'd ribbands On it I will bestow; But chiefly black and yelloweSee above, preface to No. XI. Book II. p. 178.: With her to grave shall go. Ding, &c.
I'll decke her tomb with flowers, The rarest ever seen, And with my tears, as showers, I'll keepe them fresh and green. Ding, &c.
Instead of fairest colours, Set forth with curious artThis alludes to the painted effigies of Alabaster, anciently erected upon tombs and monuments., Her image shall be painted On my distressed heart. Ding, &c.
And thereon shall be graven Her epitaph so faire, “Here lies the loveliest maiden, “That e'er gave shepheard care.” Ding, &c.
In sable will I mourne; Blacke shall be all my weede; Ay me! I am forlorne, Now Phillida is dead! Ding dong, ding dong, ding dong, My Phillida is dead! I'll stick a branch of willow At my fair Phillis' head.
